prompt: A text says: "SwiftShip: your parcel is on hold, a $1.99 redelivery fee is unpaid. Pay at swiftship-redeliver.top". What's the safest move?
options: Pay it, it's only $1.99
Reply STOP so they leave you alone
Open the official SwiftShip app or type its site yourself to check tracking
Tap the link just to see if it looks real
explanation: Tiny fees are the hook: the real goal is your card number. Check tracking through the official app or a site you type yourself. Replying confirms your number is active.

prompt: "northbridgebank.com" and "northbrigdebank.com" lead to the same website.
explanation: Look closely: "brigde" swaps two letters. Lookalike domains differ by one or two characters to fool a quick glance. Use bookmarks or the official app for banking.

prompt: Tap every red flag in this text message.

regions.why: An overseas personal number, not a toll agency short code.
Naming a real-sounding agency isn't a red flag by itself.

regions.text: Final notice! Pay within 12 hours to avoid a $50 late fee.
regions.why: Pressure + a big threatened penalty is the classic toll-scam lever.
A balance alone is normal; it's the pressure and link that give it away.
The real agency would use its own domain (metrotoll.org), not a '.icu' lookalike.

explanation: Toll scams pair a small balance with a big penalty and a lookalike link. Log in through the agency's official site or app instead.

prompt: You get a call that sounds exactly like your nephew. He's crying, says he's in trouble, and needs money sent right now. What's the best first step?
options: Send the money quickly, the voice is definitely his
Hang up and call him (or a parent) back on a number you already have
Ask him to text you his bank details
Buy gift cards so it's faster
explanation: AI tools can clone a voice from a few seconds of audio. Hang up and call back on a known number, or agree on a family code word ahead of time.

prompt: If your phone suddenly shows "No service" and you get emails about password resets you didn't request, you could be the victim of a SIM swap and should contact your carrier right away.
explanation: In a SIM swap, a criminal moves your number to their SIM so they receive your texts and codes. Call your carrier from another phone and add a port-out PIN.

prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

regions.why: The real bank's domain is northbridgebank.com; this is a lookalike.
Real banks send sign-in alerts too, so the subject alone isn't proof.
Your bank knows your name. Generic greetings suggest a mass phish.

regions.text: Your account will be suspended in 24 hours unless you verify your identity.
regions.why: Threats and deadlines push you to act before thinking.
The registered domain is account-check.xyz; the bank name is just a subdomain.
A normal sign-off.

explanation: Check the sender domain and the real registered domain of links (the part right before .com/.xyz). When in doubt, open your bank's app directly.

prompt: A parking meter has a sticker: "Pay faster! Scan this QR code." What's the main risk?
options: None, QR codes are always official
The sticker may be placed over the real one and lead to a fake payment site
QR codes can drain your battery
It will only show an ad
explanation: Scammers paste their own QR stickers on meters, menus and flyers. Check where the code leads before entering card details, or pay through the official app.

prompt: Reusing one strong password on many sites is safe as long as it's long and complex.
explanation: If any one of those sites is breached, attackers try that password everywhere (credential stuffing). Use a unique password per site with a password manager.

prompt: Tap every red flag in this recruiter text.

regions.why: A regular number isn't suspicious by itself.

regions.text: Hi! I'm Ava from Talent Bridge Staffing.
regions.why: An introduction alone isn't a red flag.

regions.text: Remote role: $450/day, no experience or interview needed.
regions.why: Very high pay for no experience and no interview is too good to be true.

regions.text: Message our manager on a private chat app to start today.
regions.why: Moving you to an encrypted chat app avoids platform safety checks.

regions.text: Please send a $60 equipment fee to begin.
regions.why: Real employers never charge you to start a job.

explanation: Fake job offers promise easy money, skip interviews, and then ask for fees, bank details or ID. Apply through the company's official careers page.

prompt: Your phone shows ten sign-in approval prompts in a row that you didn't start. What should you do?
options: Approve one so they stop
Deny them all, change your password, and report it
Turn your phone off and forget about it
Reply to the notification asking who it is
explanation: This is MFA fatigue: an attacker already has your password and is spamming prompts hoping you tap Approve. Deny, change the password, and tell your IT team or provider.

prompt: On café Wi-Fi, if your browser shows a certificate warning for your bank's site, it's fine to click "Continue anyway" because you know the site.
explanation: A certificate warning on a site you know can mean someone on the network is intercepting traffic. Disconnect and use mobile data or a trusted network instead.

prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

regions.why: MegaMart's real domain is megamart.com, not a 'rewards-center' lookalike.
You can't win a contest you never entered.

regions.text: Thanks for shopping with us this year.
regions.why: Friendly filler, not a red flag.

regions.text: Just cover $4.95 shipping. Enter your card details within 24 hours.
regions.why: A 'small fee' to claim a prize is how they get your card number.
HTML attachments often open fake login or card forms.

explanation: Real prizes don't require card details or fees. Check promotions in the store's official app.

prompt: While browsing, a pop-up says "Your browser is out of date! Download update.exe now." What should you do?
options: Download it, updates are important
Close the page and update only through your browser's settings or official app store
Call the phone number on the pop-up
Disable your antivirus first
explanation: Fake update prompts deliver malware. Browsers and operating systems update themselves through settings, never through random web pop-ups.

prompt: A real government agency or utility company may ask you to pay an overdue bill with gift cards.
explanation: No legitimate agency or utility takes gift cards as payment. Anyone demanding gift cards, crypto or wire transfers is a scammer.

prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

regions.why: A security company billing you from a free webmail address.
Receipts are normal, but check the details.

regions.text: Thank you for being a loyal customer.
regions.why: Polite filler.

regions.text: Didn't authorize this? Call our refund desk at 1-888-555-0136 within 24 hours.
regions.why: The goal is to get you on the phone and install remote-access tools.
A double extension: it's a program (.exe) pretending to be a PDF.

explanation: Fake invoices create panic so you call. Check subscriptions by signing in to the vendor's real site yourself.

prompt: Which of these links actually goes to PayWave's real site (paywave.com)?
options: paywave.com.account-verify.net/login
paywave-login.co
paywave.com/login
paywaye.com/login
explanation: Read the domain right before the first single slash: 'account-verify.net', 'paywave-login.co' and 'paywaye.com' are all different owners.

prompt: You get a code you didn't request, then someone calls "from your bank" and asks you to read it back to verify your identity. You should read it to them.
explanation: That code is the key to your account. Your bank will never ask you to read it back. Hang up and call the number on your card.

prompt: Tap every red flag in this text message.

regions.why: Texts sent from email addresses are a common smishing trick.
Brand names are easy to fake but aren't a flag on their own.

regions.text: Final attempt! Your package will be returned today.
regions.why: Urgency to stop you from double-checking.

regions.text: Pay the $2.49 handling fee to release it.
regions.why: Unexpected small fees are the bait.
'swlftship' uses an L instead of an I.

explanation: Look for lookalike spellings, email-address senders and surprise fees. Check tracking in the official app.

prompt: A friendly stranger who texted you by "wrong number" now shares screenshots of big crypto profits and offers to help you invest on a platform they recommend. This matches which growing scam pattern?
options: A legitimate mentorship
A long-con investment scam that builds trust, then traps your deposits
A bank fraud alert
A software update
explanation: These long-con scams build a relationship over weeks, show fake gains, then block withdrawals until you pay 'fees'. Only use regulated platforms you found yourself.

prompt: Someone you met online who always avoids video calls and then needs money for a medical emergency is showing common romance-scam signs.
explanation: Avoiding video, fast declarations of love and sudden emergencies are classic romance-scam patterns. Never send money to someone you haven't met in person.

prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

regions.why: Not CloudNest's real domain (cloudnest.com).
Generic greeting from a service that knows your name.

regions.text: Your mailbox is full. New messages will be deleted within 24 hours.
regions.why: Threat + deadline to rush you.
The registered domain is mail-upgrade.top.

regions.text: You're receiving this as a CloudNest member.
regions.why: Standard footer text.

explanation: 'Mailbox full' and 'password expiring' emails lead to fake logins. Open the service yourself to check storage.
